title: What Tubes Do to Results: Fluoride, Clotting Time and Gel
summary: See why a grey-top tube still loses glucose for hours, why serum tubes must clot before spinning, and how gel separators soak up drugs like phenytoin.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 3 Hits 7–9 and Traps 3–4. Adds citrate-buffered tubes and the ADA/AACC advice, the 5–7% per hour glycolysis rate, fibrin strands from early centrifugation and the size of gel drug losses. The reviewer’s “good for 3 days”, plain-red 60-minute clot time and re-spin hyperkalemia stay pending.

objectives: Explain why fluoride tubes do not protect glucose during the first hours and when citrate-buffered tubes are preferred.
State typical clotting times for silica gel tubes and thrombin tubes and the risk of spinning too early.
Name drugs absorbed by gel separators and choose an appropriate tube for therapeutic drug monitoring.

scenes.title: The grey tube that still lost sugar
scenes.altText: A grey-top fluoride tube for a glucose test sits on a counter while a clock runs two hours. A glucose bar slowly shrinks. A label asks: “Isn’t the grey top supposed to stop this?” The cartoon scientist looks puzzled.

cues.text: A glucose sample is drawn into a grey-top fluoride tube — the tube made to protect glucose.
It waits on the counter for two hours. When it is finally tested, the glucose reads lower than the patient’s real level.
Isn’t the grey top supposed to stop that? And what else can tubes do to results?

props.text: Isn’t the grey top supposed to stop this?

scenes.title: Cells keep eating glucose
scenes.altText: A glycolysis assembly line: glucose enters at the left, passes several steps and leaves as lactate. A red “fluoride” block lands on a late step (enolase) and only gradually stops the line — a timer shows full effect by about 4 hours. A second tube type, citrate-buffered fluoride, drops the pH and blocks the very first step (hexokinase) at once; its glucose bar stays flat.

cues.text: Blood cells are alive in the tube. They keep using glucose for energy — about 5 to 7 percent of it every hour at room temperature.
They break glucose down step by step on an assembly line called glycolysis, ending in lactate.
Fluoride jams a late step on that line. But it acts slowly: it does little in the first one to two hours and fully stops glycolysis only by about 4 hours.
A newer tube adds citrate buffer. It makes the blood slightly acidic, pH 5.3 to 5.9, which stops the very first step at once.
So guidelines say: if the sample can’t be iced and separated within 30 minutes, use a tube with a fast glycolysis blocker such as citrate buffer.

props.label: Cells use glucose ≈ 5–7% per hour (room temp.)
Fluoride only: glucose still falls early

scenes.title: Clotting before spinning
scenes.altText: Three serum tubes with stopwatches: a gold SST with silica clot activator (about 30–60 minutes to clot), a plain red tube (the reviewer says about 60 minutes) and a thrombin rapid-serum tube (about 5 minutes). One SST is spun too early: thin fibrin strands form in the serum and tangle an analyzer probe.

cues.text: Serum is what is left after blood clots. So serum tubes must finish clotting before they go into the centrifuge.
A gold gel tube with silica clot activator takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes. The reviewer gives about 30 for gel tubes and about 60 for plain red tubes.
Thrombin rapid-serum tubes clot in about 5 minutes — useful when results are urgent.
Spin a tube before it has clotted, and clotting continues in the serum. Thin fibrin strands form.
Fibrin strands can clog or fool the analyzer’s sampling probe, giving wrong results or errors. Wait for the clot.

props.label: Spun too early → clot keeps forming
Strands clog or fool the sampling probe ✗

scenes.title: In the lab: gel that drinks drugs
scenes.altText: A gold gel tube in close-up: drug molecules (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, quinidine, lidocaine) drift from the serum into the gel layer, and a drug-level bar falls over time. A card: losses as large as 20–50% after 24 hours at 4 °C. A green check marks a no-gel tube for therapeutic drug monitoring. A last token warns that re-spinning a gel tube can raise potassium.

cues.text: Gel separator tubes have a plug of gel that sits between cells and serum after spinning. Handy — but the gel is not completely inert.
Some fat-loving drugs soak into the gel: phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, quinidine and lidocaine.
The longer the serum sits on the gel, the more drug is lost — as much as 20 to 50 percent after 24 hours in the fridge in one review.
So for therapeutic drug monitoring of these drugs, use a tube without gel, such as a plain red tube.
One more gel caution from the reviewer: spinning a gel tube a second time can push potassium up — a pseudohyperkalemia.

props.text: Serum sits on the gel layer
Up to 20–50% lost after 24 h at 4 °C

props.label: TDM: use a tube without gel ✓

scenes.title: Traps: instant fluoride and inert gel
scenes.altText: Two trap cards are crossed out: “Grey tops stop glycolysis instantly” → “Fluoride takes hours; citrate buffer is immediate.” “Gel is inert, so it’s fine for TDM” → “Gel absorbs some drugs — use no-gel tubes.” A third token: “Spin only after clotting.”

cues.text: Trap one: “Grey-top fluoride tubes stop glycolysis the moment blood enters.” No — fluoride takes hours. Early glucose loss still happens; citrate-buffered tubes act at once.
Trap two: “Gel is inert, so gel tubes are fine for drug levels.” No — gel absorbs phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, quinidine and lidocaine over time.
And a timing rule: spin serum tubes only after they have clotted — about 30 to 60 minutes for silica gel tubes, about 5 for thrombin tubes.

And: gel grabs greasy drugs — the fat-loving ones like phenytoin.
Where it breaks: glucose loss also depends on temperature and white-cell count, not all drugs bind gel, and how much is absorbed depends on time, temperature and the gel itself.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Fluoride: slow (≈ 4 h)”, “Clot first, then spin”, “TDM: no gel”.

cues.text: Tubes change results: fluoride needs hours to stop glycolysis, so early glucose still falls unless a citrate-buffered tube is used; serum tubes must clot before spinning; and gel tubes soak up some drugs, so drug levels go in tubes without gel.

explanation.what: Plain language: blood cells keep eating sugar in the tube; the grey-top chemical slows this only after a few hours; serum tubes need time to clot; and the gel in some tubes soaks up certain medicines. Scientific terms: glycolysis continues in vitro (≈ 5–7% per hour at room temperature); sodium fluoride inhibits glycolysis with a delay of up to ~4 hours; citrate buffer (pH 5.3–5.9) inhibits it immediately. Silica clot activators need ~30–60 minutes, thrombin tubes ~5 minutes. Hydrophobic drugs adsorb to gel separators.
explanation.why: Fluoride blocks a late glycolysis step and acts slowly, so glucose continues to fall early; acidifying citrate buffer blocks the first step at once. Centrifuging before clotting is complete lets clotting continue in the serum, forming fibrin strands. Fat-soluble drugs move from serum into the hydrophobic gel over time.
explanation.measure: Labs see falsely low glucose in delayed fluoride samples, probe errors or erratic results from fibrin, and falsely low drug levels (up to 20–50% loss after 24 h at 4 °C in one review) from gel tubes.
explanation.differs: Fluoride vs citrate-buffered fluoride: delayed vs immediate glycolysis inhibition. Silica SST vs thrombin tube: ~30–60 min vs ~5 min to clot. Gel tube vs plain red tube: convenient separation vs no drug absorption.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “glucose in a grey top after 2 h is…” (falsely low), the ~4 h fluoride delay, which tube for phenytoin levels (no gel), clotting times before centrifugation, and the trap that gel is inert.

points: Absorbs phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, quinidine, lidocaine

right.label: No-gel tube
points: Preferred for TDM of these drugs

comparisons.distinguisher: Whether a hydrophobic gel touches the serum.

mnemonic.text: Fluoride is slow, citrate is now — and gel grabs greasy drugs.
mnemonic.explanation: Fluoride takes hours to stop glycolysis; citrate buffer stops it at once. Gel soaks up fat-loving (greasy) drugs like phenytoin.
mnemonic.limitation: Glucose loss also depends on temperature and white-cell count. Not every drug binds gel, and the amount absorbed depends on time, temperature and the specific gel. The aid says nothing about clotting times.

analogyLimitations: The glycolysis “assembly line” shows only a few of its ten steps.
Drug “molecules” sinking into the gel are drawn far larger than real molecules.
Shrinking bars show direction, not exact amounts.
takeaway: Tubes change results: fluoride needs hours to stop glycolysis, so early glucose still falls unless a citrate-buffered tube is used; serum tubes must clot before spinning; and gel tubes soak up some drugs, so drug levels go in tubes without gel.

questions.stem: A glucose sample in a sodium fluoride (grey-top) tube sat at room temperature for 2 hours before separation. What is the most likely effect?

options.text: Falsely low glucose, because fluoride has little effect during the first 1–2 hours
options.rationale: Correct. Glycolysis continues early; fluoride’s full effect takes up to about 4 hours.

options.text: No change, because fluoride stops glycolysis instantly
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the classic trap; fluoride’s action is delayed.

options.text: Falsely high glucose from fluoride interference
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cells consume glucose, so the error is downward.

options.text: Falsely low glucose, because fluoride destroys glucose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fluoride does not destroy glucose; living cells consume it.

questions.stem: Which tube is most appropriate for a phenytoin trough level?

options.rationale: Correct. Gel separators absorb hydrophobic drugs such as phenytoin, so a tube without gel is used.

options.text: A gold gel separator tube, spun quickly
options.rationale: Incorrect. Gel absorption is time-dependent but still a risk; no-gel tubes are preferred.
Incorrect. Fluoride tubes are for glucose (and lactate), not drug monitoring.
Incorrect. Citrate tubes are for coagulation testing.

questions.stem: A gold SST with silica clot activator is centrifuged 5 minutes after collection. What problem is most likely?

options.text: Fibrin strands in the serum that interfere with sampling
options.rationale: Correct. Silica activators need roughly 30–60 minutes; spinning early lets clotting continue in the serum.
Incorrect. Early spinning does not raise glucose; delayed spinning lowers it.
Incorrect. Gel absorption lowers drug levels over time; early spinning does not raise them.

options.text: No problem, because all serum tubes clot in 5 minutes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only thrombin rapid-serum tubes clot in about 5 minutes.

claims.text: Glycolysis consumes glucose at about 5–7% per hour at room temperature.
Sodium fluoride has little effect in the first 1–2 h and fully inhibits glycolysis by about 4 h.
Citrate buffer (pH 5.3–5.9) inhibits glycolysis immediately; guidelines advise it when samples cannot be iced and separated within 30 minutes.
Silica clot activators need about 30–60 min; thrombin rapid tubes about 5 min; spinning before clotting leaves fibrin that interferes with sampling.
Gel separators absorb phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, quinidine and lidocaine in a time-dependent way (20–50% after 24 h at 4 °C), so no-gel tubes are preferred for their TDM.
Fluoride inhibits enolase (via a fluoride–magnesium complex), a late glycolytic step.
claims.note: Standard biochemistry; not stated in the passages read.

claims.text: Fluoride preserves glucose for 3 days; unseparated fluoride specimens still lose 0.39 mmol/L.
claims.note: WHO 2010 says “up to five days” (register flag rv-fluoride-days); the 0.39 mmol/L figure was not found.

claims.text: Plain red tubes need about 60 min to clot; re-centrifuging a gel tube causes pseudohyperkalemia.
claims.note: Bowen 2014 notes RBCs crossing the gel can raise potassium, but not re-spinning specifically.

claims.text: “Fluoride is slow, citrate is now — gel grabs greasy drugs.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Reviewer: fluoride “good for 3 days”; WHO 2010: “up to five days”.
The reviewer does not mention citrate-buffered tubes, which current guidance prefers when samples cannot be cooled and separated promptly.
